title: New Year in Tokyo 2027: 3 temples and shrines to plan your visit
description: Plan New Year in Tokyo 2027 with Senso-ji, Meiji Jingu and Zojoji: the updated bell ceremony, transport checks, reservations and a sensible itinerary.
relatedQueries: where to spend New Year in Tokyo
intro: For New Year in Tokyo, from December 31, 2026 into January 1, 2027, choose one temple for the evening and leave a separate visit for the following day. Senso-ji provides the Buddhist setting of Asakusa; Meiji Jingu introduces hatsumode, the first shrine visit of the year; Zojoji offers an important confirmed change to its year-end bell ceremony. Trying to fit all three into the same few hours makes the experience depend on transfers and queues rather than the places themselves.

This guide helps you choose between a religious New Year visit, a daylight walk and a ceremony with a specifically announced time. Research was checked on November 12, 2026. The dated Zojoji announcement is treated separately from annual traditions and pages that still refer to January 2026. That distinction matters when booking a night around an event. The documentary photographs identify the places; they do not show the forthcoming 2027 celebration.

sections.heading: 1. Senso-ji: welcome the year in the Asakusa of Kannon
paragraphs: Senso-ji suits a visitor who wants more than a photograph at midnight. Its history centres on Kannon, the Buddhist figure of compassion, and the approach brings together Kaminarimon Gate, Nakamise shopping street, Hozomon Gate, the pagoda and the main hall. The principal Kannon image remains concealed: entering the temple does not mean seeing that statue. Paying attention to the gates and the layout gives the visit substance even when crowd management limits where you can stop.

The temple’s annual calendar places its major New Year prayers between January 1 and January 7 and describes the traditional start of rites as the year changes. This is religious context, not a fast-entry booking or a promise that every visitor can approach the bell. Check dated notices for January 2027 before setting out. Ordinary main-hall opening times do not establish exceptional New Year’s Eve arrangements. A daylight visit is a sensible choice for families or anyone who would rather avoid making a long wait at midnight the centre of the trip.

Keep shopping and worship as separate parts of the outing. Walk through Nakamise when individual shops are open, then keep the approach to the temple clear. Queues, browsing and a meal mean a real visit takes longer than a map’s walking estimate. Save your accommodation address and an alternative route out of the area. Follow the temple’s instructions during prayer; Senso-ji follows a Buddhist tradition, so do not automatically copy the hand-clapping associated with a Shinto shrine.

sections.heading: 2. Meiji Jingu: make time for hatsumode and the shrine approach
paragraphs: Hatsumode does not require reaching a gate at exactly midnight. GO TOKYO explains that people also make the visit on January 1, 2 or 3. Meiji Jingu describes it as gratitude for the past year and fresh intentions for the next. This flexibility lets you rest the night before and visit with greater attention the following morning. The wooded approaches are part of the outing rather than a corridor to rush through for a single photograph.

The shrine makes an easily missed distinction: the station-to-entrance journey is followed by at least another ten minutes on foot to the main buildings in normal conditions. The southern approach is associated with Harajuku and Meiji-jingumae; the official precinct map also shows approaches from Yoyogi, Kita-sando and Sangubashi. Choose an entrance before travelling and follow any special route in operation. Wheelchairs are listed as available at entrances, but availability and a suitable route should be checked for your circumstances instead of being treated as a guaranteed reservation.

At the November review, the special hatsumode page still contained references to Reiwa 8 and the horse of 2026. Its overnight timetable and participation conditions are therefore not presented here as a 2027 announcement. The general visitor page confirms daily free access to the shrine grounds, with regular hours following daylight; individual facilities can have their own arrangements. Read current notices before choosing a night visit. A confirmed daytime visit is more dependable than planning around a late opening that belongs to the previous season.

sections.heading: 3. Zojoji: the year-end bell ceremony now starts earlier
paragraphs: Zojoji is particularly useful for travellers who want to plan December 31 around a dated announcement. The official notice of November 1, 2026 sets the ceremony at 21:30, the start of bell ringing at 21:45 and an expected finish around 23:00. This brings the event forward from the previous ceremony at 23:45 and ringing from midnight. Arriving for a first strike at twelve could mean missing it. Allow time to reach the temple and reread the current notice shortly before your visit.

The same notice says the publicly distributed allocation of bell-ringing tickets is scheduled to become available from December 1 at 09:00 at the second-floor office of the meeting building. This does not guarantee availability, online purchase or participation without a ticket. If personally ringing the bell is your priority, read the full linked conditions before building the trip around it. Watching a ceremony and taking part in the ringing are separate activities; a hotel booking is not evidence that either form of access has been secured.

The setting combines the history of Jodo Buddhism and the Tokugawa family with the outline of Tokyo Tower. One visual expectation needs adjusting: Sangedatsumon Gate is undergoing conservation. GO TOKYO gives a planned completion in November 2032, so an older archive photograph does not show its present condition. Onarimon on the Toei Mita Line is an officially listed approach, but the published walking time does not include queues. Visit in daylight for the architecture and return only if the announced ceremony arrangements suit your evening.

sections.heading: Choose the evening and the first January visits separately
paragraphs: With only one evening, select Zojoji if the announced bell schedule is your main interest, or concentrate on Asakusa and check Senso-ji’s own New Year notices. Leave Meiji Jingu for a different outing. These places are in separate parts of Tokyo; transfers and queues matter more than the number of names on a list. A late dinner, a cross-city journey and a fixed ceremony time leave little room for delays if all three are squeezed together.

With two days, a temple on December 31 and a shrine on January 1 or 2 is a more balanced combination, always within confirmed access arrangements. The trip does not become more complete through repeated lengthy queues. Spare time allows you to look around, eat comfortably and return before fatigue makes the journey difficult. Visiting after midnight does not miss the tradition: the official tourism guide explicitly recognises hatsumode during the first several days of the year.

sections.heading: Transport and accommodation: work out the return journey first
paragraphs: Before booking, choose accommodation with a manageable return from your preferred temple or shrine and check the relevant operators’ last services for your exact date. A metro map proves that lines connect, not that they will operate all night on December 31, 2026. No special overnight trains are assumed in this guide. If extra services are announced later, check the stations served and the final leg to your accommodation as well as the headline announcement.

Save the route and your address in Japanese so the plan does not depend on continuous mobile reception. At Meiji Jingu, add the walk inside the grounds after reaching the entrance; for Zojoji, study the Onarimon approach and ceremony instructions. Agree on a meeting point outside the main flow of people. For children, older relatives or travellers with limited mobility, a daytime visit and an early return reduce the decisions that would otherwise have to be made while standing in a crowd.

sections.heading: Bookings, food and the costs to keep separate
paragraphs: Book accommodation and, if a particular dinner matters to you, confirm its December 31 opening and conditions directly. Do not budget on the assumption that every shop opens on January 1: GO TOKYO warns of closures that day. Keep a meal alternative near your hotel and check whether it needs a reservation. There is no single price for New Year in Tokyo. Transport, dinner, shopping, donations and optional activities belong in separate parts of the budget.

For the religious sites, distinguish walking through the grounds, worshipping and requesting a particular service or activity. Meiji Jingu’s ordinary free access does not mean every facility or service is included, and Zojoji has its own announced ticket-distribution mechanism for bell ringing. Be cautious about any intermediary promising ceremonial access without explaining the authorisation. Operator conditions and current seasonal notices should guide the decision rather than photographs or stories from a different year.

sections.heading: Cold-weather preparation, photography and visiting respectfully
paragraphs: Bring layers, walking shoes and gloves that let you consult your phone. Standing still feels different from walking continuously, so plan an indoor break before and after a ceremony, particularly with children. The official January guide recommends warm clothing, but its previous-year averages are not a forecast for your night. Check the local forecast close to the trip and shorten the outing if rain, wind or discomfort would make waiting unpleasant.

A temple or shrine remains a place of worship during a holiday. Do not stop for photographs in the middle of a moving queue or block an entrance, and check each area’s camera restrictions. Put the camera away when requested. Senso-ji provides a Buddhist setting and Meiji Jingu a Shinto one; recognising the difference improves the visit. Following the staff’s instructions is more useful than trying to reproduce a video recorded during a previous New Year celebration.

itinerary: December 31: choose one area and see its temple in daylight. If choosing Zojoji, eat early and allow a comfortable margin before the ceremony announced for 21:30. Check both the return journey and the latest notice before leaving. With ringing expected to end around 23:00, decide separately how to spend midnight instead of assuming the temple promises a midnight show.

January 1 or 2: visit Meiji Jingu independently within the confirmed 2027 arrangements, or choose a daytime Senso-ji visit if it remains on your list. Allow a meal break and a flexible afternoon. Our Tokyo and Kyoto guides can help extend the broader trip; Christmas in Tokyo covers a different part of the season and does not establish New Year access conditions.

faq.question: Must I visit a temple at exactly midnight?
faq.answer: No. Hatsumode also takes place on January 1, 2 and 3. A daylight visit within confirmed opening arrangements is a valid alternative and can be easier if you prefer not to organise a late-night return.

faq.question: When is the Zojoji bell ceremony on December 31, 2026?
faq.answer: The November 1, 2026 notice announces the ceremony at 21:30, ringing from 21:45 and an expected finish around 23:00. This changes the previous schedule. Check the notice again before travelling to the temple.

faq.question: Is Meiji Jingu’s overnight opening confirmed for 2027?
faq.answer: At our November 12 review, the special page still showed Reiwa 8 information, referring to 2026. Those hours are not treated as a 2027 confirmation. Read the shrine’s latest announcements before choosing an overnight visit.

faq.question: Are all-night trains and a Shibuya countdown guaranteed?
faq.answer: Neither is assumed for the change from 2026 to 2027 in this guide. Plan the return with checked operator timetables and do not book on the basis of a street celebration or transport arrangement announced for a previous year.

conclusion: A good New Year plan in Tokyo starts with one religious priority and a return journey you can manage. Zojoji has a newly announced schedule, Senso-ji provides the traditions of Asakusa, and Meiji Jingu gives hatsumode its shrine setting. Separate the outings and confirm access and transport rather than trying to visit all three in the same night.
